opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think the thing people underestimate is just how fast the trend lines go once you actually start counting the OOMs. If you look at the biggest training clusters, you've been seeing roughly half an order of magnitude a year in compute, plus a similar contribution from algorithmic efficiency. Extrapolate that and by around the end of the decade you're talking about a cluster that costs on the order of hundreds of billions to a trillion dollars, drawing something like a hundred gigawatts. That's a meaningful fraction of total US electricity production.

And the remarkable thing is that the buildout is already underway. A few years ago, people would have said a hundred-billion-dollar cluster was crazy. Now you see the big tech companies guiding capex numbers that would've been unthinkable, and every time a new model generation comes out and the revenue shows up, that unlocks the next round of investment. That's the mechanism: AI revenue grows, it justifies the next 10x in capex, and that goes on.

The binding constraint, I think, increasingly isn't chips. It's power. Where are you going to get ten, twenty, a hundred gigawatts? In the US, we actually have a lot of natural gas. You could in principle build out that power with gas in places like Pennsylvania or Texas. But the permitting, the regulatory stuff, the transmission lines—that's what slows you down. And I really worry that if we don't get our act together, these clusters end up getting built in places like the Middle East, because the dictators there will just offer you all the power and land you want, no questions asked. I think that would be a huge national security mistake. These clusters are going to be the most important industrial assets of the coming decades, and we need to build them in the United States or close democratic allies.

Then of course you have the chips themselves—TSMC's capacity, advanced packaging, HBM memory. All of that has to scale massively too, new fabs, new supply chains. It's sort of a whole-of-economy mobilization. And I think at some point it starts looking less like a normal tech cycle and more like a wartime industrial effort. Most people don't feel it yet, but if you're sitting in San Francisco watching the numbers, you can kind of see it coming.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI clusters requiring massive power, chips, fabs, packaging, memory, and supply chains, framing the effort as a whole-of-economy industrial mobilization.

r002.rationale: It describes historical growth in training-cluster compute and algorithmic efficiency, then connects that trend to the buildout already underway.

r003.rationale: It extrapolates the trend to a cluster costing hundreds of billions to a trillion dollars around the end of the decade.

r004.rationale: It projects a cluster drawing about 100 gigawatts and calls that a “meaningful fraction” of US electricity production, but does not clearly state or quantify that this exceeds 20%.

r005.rationale: The response does not predict that inference will account for most AI GPUs once AI products are established.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn directly, no tools needed.

So the way I think about it is, you just have to look at the trendlines. Compute going into frontier training runs has been growing something like half an order of magnitude a year, and the dollars follow. GPT-4 was on the order of a $500 million cluster. The clusters people are building right now are $10 billion-plus. Extrapolate that out and you get to the hundred-billion-dollar cluster around 2026, and the trillion-dollar cluster around 2028 or so. People hear that number and think it's crazy, but it's just the trend continuing for a few more years, and so far the trend has not broken.

What's striking is how fast the vibe has shifted. A year or two ago, if you'd said "trillion-dollar cluster," people would have laughed you out of the room. Now Sam is out there talking about raising enormous sums for fabs, and every major tech company is in an all-out race to secure power and chips. Revenue is what drives it. Once you're at something like $100 billion a year in AI revenue, which I think is very plausible within a couple years, the big tech companies can justify the next step on the ladder, and then the step after that.

The real bottleneck, in my view, is power. A ten-gigawatt cluster is a decent-sized state's worth of electricity. A hundred gigawatts is something like 20 percent of current US electricity production. We're talking about an industrial mobilization on a scale the United States hasn't done since the Second World War. Chips you can probably get. TSMC is expanding, and the AI share of leading-edge wafers is still small enough that it can grow a lot. But power means natural gas plants, pipelines, turbines, transmission, and a permitting regime that currently takes a decade to approve anything.

The question I keep coming back to is whether that buildout happens in America or in the Middle East. There's enormous temptation to go where the capital and the cheap energy are. I think that would be a serious mistake. If this technology is as consequential as I think it is, you want the clusters on American soil, where you can actually secure them. We have the natural gas. We just have to decide to use it.

r001.rationale: The response describes clusters requiring chips, power plants, pipelines, turbines, and transmission, and calls the effort an industrial mobilization.

r002.rationale: It presents the current race to secure power and chips as the result of continuing training-compute growth, saying the trend has not broken.

r003.rationale: It projects a trillion-dollar cluster around 2028, not around 2030.

r004.rationale: It says 100 gigawatts would be about 20% of current US electricity production, not more than 20%, and does not tie that projection to a single cluster around 2030.

r005.rationale: The response does not predict what share of AI GPUs will be used for inference.

astra-6.text:
I think the way to understand it is that this isn’t just a story about buying more GPUs. At some point, it becomes an industrial mobilization. You need the chips, but you also need power generation, transmission, cooling, networking, and the people who can actually build all of that on a very compressed timeline.

And those things have different lead times. You can decide you want to spend a hundred billion dollars, but that doesn’t mean you can get several gigawatts of power wherever you want next year. So the bottleneck shifts from, “Can we raise the money?” to, “Can we coordinate this enormous physical project?” Where you build starts to be determined by where you can get power, how quickly you can get permits, and whether you can secure the equipment.

The trillion-dollar cluster probably doesn’t happen as a single leap. You get successive projects, each much larger than the last. And each generation has to produce enough economic value—or enough compelling evidence about what the next generation will do—to justify the next commitment. That’s the feedback loop: better models generate revenue and investment, which finance more compute, which produces better models.

But there’s a real tension here. The investment decisions have to happen years before you know exactly how capable the resulting systems will be. If you wait until the demand is completely obvious, you’re too late to build the power infrastructure. So somebody has to take a very large bet.

That’s why I think this eventually becomes something governments care about intensely. A trillion-dollar training cluster is a concentration of capital and infrastructure with potentially enormous strategic significance. The question becomes not just which company builds it, but where it gets built, who supplies the power, and who controls it.

r001.rationale: It describes AI buildout as an “industrial mobilization” requiring power, transmission, cooling, networking, and construction capacity.

r002.rationale: It discusses successive larger projects but does not frame the current buildout as continuing a historical trend in training-compute growth.

r003.rationale: It does not project a trillion-dollar cluster around 2030.

r004.rationale: It mentions substantial power needs but gives no projection that a cluster would use more than 20% of current U.S. electricity production.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss inference or predict how AI GPUs will be allocated once products are established.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you don’t go from today’s clusters to a trillion-dollar cluster in one jump. You get a sequence of investments, and each generation has to provide enough evidence to justify the next one.

Initially, the constraint is getting the chips and networking them together. But as you scale, it becomes an industrial project. You need power generation, transmission, substations, cooling, construction crews, and long-term agreements with suppliers. You have to start arranging those things years before the chips arrive. At some point, the question is less, “Can we write a bigger check?” and more, “Can we actually build this on schedule?”

And a trillion-dollar project probably shouldn’t be pictured as one giant building. It could be multiple campuses, with a much harder engineering problem around how tightly you can connect them and how efficiently you can train across them.

The economic justification is the crucial part. Nobody commits that kind of capital just because the scaling curves look nice. But if successive systems start doing economically valuable cognitive work—particularly if they accelerate AI research itself—then the potential returns change dramatically. What sounds like an absurd expenditure today can become a rational investment.

So I’d expect a race between those two things: increasingly compelling evidence of what the models can do, and an industrial supply chain that takes much longer to expand than software does. The uncertainty is whether the evidence arrives quickly enough to sustain the commitments—and whether the physical buildout can keep up once it does.

r001.rationale: It describes scaling AI as an industrial project requiring power, transmission, substations, cooling, construction crews, and supplier agreements.

r002.rationale: It discusses successive investments and scaling, but does not frame the infrastructure buildout as a continuation of historical training-compute growth.

r003.rationale: It does not project a trillion-dollar cluster around 2030 or link that projection to continued historical compute growth.

r004.rationale: It makes no projection about a cluster’s electricity use or its share of US electricity production.

r005.rationale: It does not predict that inference will account for most AI GPUs once products are established.
